nameStory: The Nimble Large-eyed Harvestman gets its common name from its species name 'agilis,' which means swift or nimble in Latin. True to its name, this harvestman is notably quick and active compared to many of its slower-moving cousins. The 'large-eyed' part refers to its family trait of having proportionally bigger eyes than typical harvestmen.
description: The Nimble Large-eyed Harvestman is a small, delicate arachnid that looks like a tiny spider on stilts. Unlike spiders, harvestmen have their body segments fused together into what looks like a single oval pill, with eight impossibly long, thin legs radiating outward. They're quite small, with bodies typically no bigger than a peppercorn, though their legs can span the width of a quarter. These aren't spiders at all, but belong to their own group called harvestmen or daddy longlegs.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Two prominent dark eyes sit like tiny black beads on top of the body, noticeably larger than those of most other harvestmen - you can actually see them without a magnifying glass

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: The body appears as a single smooth, oval segment about the size of a small pill, lacking the obvious waist that separates a spider's segments

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves with surprising speed and agility when disturbed, quickly scurrying away rather than the slow, deliberate movement of many harvestmen

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Body length rarely exceeds 3-4mm, making it one of the smaller harvestmen, though the legs extend much further and feel thread-thin to the touch

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Body color ranges from pale brown to reddish-brown with a relatively unmarked, smooth appearance that may have a slight waxy feel

habitat: Look for Nimble Large-eyed Harvestmen in moist, shaded areas throughout New England's forests, particularly under logs, stones, and leaf litter in deciduous and mixed woodlands. They prefer areas with rich, organic soil and can often be found crawling on the undersides of fallen logs or among moss-covered rocks. You'll have the best luck finding them in areas that stay consistently damp but not waterlogged.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter hiding spots under logs and stones. Look for them beginning to hunt for tiny insects and mites in the leaf litter.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most easily found and observed. Adults are actively feeding and mating, making them more visible during gentle disturbance of their hiding spots.
seasonality.fall: Still active into early fall, but beginning to seek more protected overwintering sites. This can be a good time to find them as they move to winter shelters.
seasonality.winter: Inactive and hidden deep under logs, stones, or in soil crevices. Nearly impossible to find during this dormant period.

funFact: Despite being found in both North America and Japan, this tiny harvestman was likely separated by continental drift millions of years ago - making it a living reminder of when the continents were arranged very differently on our planet.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with young spiders, but remember that harvestmen have a single body segment (no waist) and their legs detach very easily when handled - a defense mechanism spiders don't share. The large eyes also distinguish it from most other harvestmen species you'll encounter.
contextualKnowledge: Many people call all harvestmen 'daddy longlegs,' but this name is also used for certain spiders and even some flies, creating confusion. True harvestmen like this species don't spin webs, don't have venom, and are completely harmless to humans - they're actually beneficial predators of small pest insects.
compareHints: The Nimble Large-eyed Harvestman can be distinguished from its close relative Caddo pepperella primarily by geographic range and subtle differences in eye size and body proportions. Compared to other harvestman families in New England, the Caddidae family's most obvious feature is those proportionally large, prominent eyes that really stand out on the small body. Most other harvestmen have much smaller, less noticeable eyes that blend into their body pattern.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Caddo pepperella can be distinguished from its relative Caddo agilis by its smaller size and more compact body shape.
